newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS -UK's George gives coded interest rate clues.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -UK's George gives coded interest rate clues.

text.p: Will he, won't he? Bank of England Governor Eddie George found himself in the glare of the media spotlight three times on Wednesday but still left economists puzzling over the chances of an imminent UK interest rate rise.
George took the unusual step of appearing on BBC radio early on Wednesday, primarily to react to the new government's plans for one super-regulator for the City of London.
But he also took time to say that while Britain's short-term inflation outlook was benign, the Bank's role was to pre-empt future pressures.

"That's what we're about, pre-emptive action to moderate the pace of the upswing...rather than leave it too little, too late," he said, adding that domestic demand was spiralling at an unsustainable rate.
He pursued the theme of acting soon enough in his foreword to the Bank's annual report, also released on Wednesday.

He acknowledged the strength of the pound -- up 17 percent in nine months -- posed a dilemma. The fact it hurts exporters by pushing their prices up but subdues short-term inflation by cutting import prices, should not be ignored, he said.
"But nor can we expose the whole of the rest of the economy to inflationary risks which would then need to be addressed by a more abrupt tightening of policy at a later stage."

Interest rate speculation rarely dips below fever pitch in London's financial markets but it has soared to new heights since Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown two weeks ago gave the Bank freedom to set interest rates.
A new, nine-strong monetary policy committee will meet for the first time next month. The Bank will have five members and the government will have no vote.

Given recent experience, where former Chancellor of the Exhequer Kenneth Clarke resisted the Bank's rate rise calls for months in a row, the fear is an unfettered central bank will tighten monetary policy further than would have otherwise been the case, and maybe too far for the good of the economy.

John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, said that was an easy argument to construct -- all central bankers are inflation hawks and now they have their heads, rates will go much higher.
"But with power comes responsibility and I expect they will exercise that cautiously," he said. "You can overstretch the argument that rates are now destined to head much higher."
Barely an hour after George's radio interview, the Treasury released minutes of his last monetary meeting with Clarke. They showed the rates argument persisted when the pair met in April.
George urged Clarke to put up rates at once but the former Chancellor rejected his advice, as he had throughout the early part of the year.

Gordon Brown acceded to George's wish on May 6, raising base rates to 6.25 percent after just five days in office, but there is no guarantee inflation hawks at the Bank of England will see that as sufficient to rein in the inflationary threat.
"The Bank will continue to...maintain the pressure for tighter policy," said HSBC Markets economist Jonathan Loynes.

At their last meeting, Clarke and George also quibbled about the strength of the pound. Clarke said it would have a similar affect to a rise in interest rates. But George said while it was dampening costs and prices in the short-term, it was having less of an effect than might have been expected.
While it is difficult to distill a concrete message from all that, it appears interest rates could go up at any time.

But conversely, Brown could stay George's hand one last time even though he has ceded control of monetary policy. Economists say the Bank is awaiting the new Chancellor's budget, due within weeks, in the hope that he will raise taxes to take the steam out of the domestic economy.
The Bank's admission that the pound is hurting manufacturers and provides a short-term dilemma for monetary policy, is a clearly coded message to Brown, they say.
"They are saying as explicitly as they can that if the government puts taxes up they will not raise rates too far," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel.

Shepperd said there was a strong case for the Bank waiting for Brown's budget before acting again. "It's probably the most important remaining piece of economic news for this year. But they will probably put up interest rates up soon afterwards."

Wednesday's economic data showing broad money supply growth dipped to 10.4 percent year-on-year in April from 11.2 in March, did little to clarify the picture even though the Bank has long pointed to M4 as an important harbinger of inflation.

"M4 probably needs to show growth below nine percent for the central bank to feel genuinely comfortable," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica. But he too thought a June rate rise was unlikely, with Brown's budget looming and measures to rein in personal spending likely.
